title: Balance Sheet
in30Seconds: A balance sheet is a financial statement that shows what a business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and what is left for its owners (equity) at a single moment in time. It is a snapshot, dated “as of” one specific day, not a report of activity over a period like the income statement. Its items are grouped into current (within one year) and non-current (beyond one year) sections, and the two sides always match: assets equal liabilities plus equity.
whyItMatters: Every serious question about a business starts with where it stands right now: can it pay what it owes soon, how much debt is it carrying, and what would the owners actually take away if it stopped tomorrow? The balance sheet is the report that answers those questions. Lenders read it before approving a loan, suppliers before extending credit, owners to see what their stake is worth, and managers to spot problems early. Reading one correctly also protects you from being impressed by size alone — a big company can sit on a weak balance sheet. It is the foundation for the ratio analysis and lending decisions you will meet in later lessons.
learningObjectives: Define the balance sheet as a snapshot: a financial statement that reports what a business owns, owes, and is worth on a specific date.
Explain the shape of the balance sheet as the accounting equation in statement form, with assets on one side and liabilities plus equity on the other.
Distinguish a point-in-time statement from a period statement, contrasting the balance sheet with the income statement.
Classify balance sheet items into current and non-current sections using the one-year horizon.
Explain what owners and lenders each look for when they read a balance sheet.
Evaluate the honest framing that a balance sheet always balances by construction and that the real question is what the numbers mean.

collegeVersion.heading: What a balance sheet is (the snapshot)
collegeVersion.body: OpenStax’s Principles of Accounting describes the balance sheet as a statement that lists what the organization owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and what it is worth (equity) on a specific date. Corporate Finance Institute calls it a snapshot of what a company owns, what it owes, and the value left for the owners. Two words in those definitions carry the whole idea: specific date. The balance sheet is a photograph, not a movie. It shows the financial position of a business at one chosen moment — the close of business on a particular day — and that day is printed at the top of the statement, usually written “as of” a date. Change any transaction after that moment and the picture would be slightly different. This is why the balance sheet is sometimes called the statement of financial position: it answers the question “where does this business stand right now?”, not “how did it get here?”

collegeVersion.heading: The shape: the equation in statement form
collegeVersion.body: The balance sheet has two sides. On one side sit the assets: cash, inventory, equipment, buildings, and everything else the business owns or controls. On the other side sit the liabilities — what the business owes to others — and equity, the owners’ claim on what remains. The two sides always match because the statement is simply the accounting equation written out: assets = liabilities + equity. The equation itself, why it holds, and how transactions keep it in balance are a separate topic covered in its own lesson. What matters here is the shape: the balance sheet is the equation in statement form, with total assets on one side and total liabilities plus total equity on the other, so the bottom lines always agree. A statement that did not balance would mean the accounting records behind it were wrong.

collegeVersion.heading: The moment in time
collegeVersion.body: The most important habit when reading a balance sheet is to notice the date. The income statement reports what happened over a period — a month, a quarter, a year — and OpenStax describes it as a statement of financial performance for a given period of time. The balance sheet works the opposite way: it reports position at the close of business on one specific date, so it is a snapshot, not a period report. A balance sheet dated December 31 shows the business as it stood at that instant; everything that happened in January is invisible to it. Comparing snapshots — last year’s balance sheet against this year’s — is how you see change over time, but any single balance sheet is frozen at one moment.

collegeVersion.heading: Current and non-current sections
collegeVersion.body: Inside each side, items are grouped by time. Current assets are expected to be used up or converted to cash within one year, and current liabilities are expected to be settled within one year. Everything that works on a longer horizon goes into the non-current sections: non-current assets such as buildings, equipment, and land, and non-current liabilities such as long-term loans and mortgages. OpenStax stresses why the split matters: knowing a business owes $750,000 is useful, but knowing that only $125,000 of it is due within a year is far more useful. The current sections show what the business can mobilize soon against what it must pay soon — the near-term pressure point of the whole statement.

collegeVersion.heading: Reading a balance sheet: owners and lenders
collegeVersion.body: Owners and lenders read the same statement for different reasons. Owners look at equity, the value left for them after subtracting what the business owes; it is their stake, built from what they invested plus profit the business kept. Lenders look at the other side of the picture: what the business owes, and especially whether its current assets can cover what comes due in the near term. A lender weighing a one-year loan wants to know whether the borrower will have the cash when the payment lands. CFI summarizes the statement’s purpose as helping investors, lenders, and leaders assess performance, funding needs, and overall financial strength — the same document, three different questions.

collegeVersion.heading: Balance sheet versus income statement, and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: The contrast between the two statements is simple: the income statement is the period report (revenues minus expenses over time), and the balance sheet is the snapshot (position at a moment). The honest framing follows from the shape itself. Because the balance sheet is built from the accounting equation, it always balances — the two sides match by construction, whether the company is thriving or struggling. That means a balanced statement is not praise; it is arithmetic. The real question is what the numbers mean: whether the assets are productive, whether the debt is manageable, and whether the equity is real value or a thin cushion. Analysts use the balance sheet to assess liquidity, financial strength, and leverage — the meaning behind the matching totals.

vocabulary.definition: A financial statement that reports what a business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and what is left for its owners (equity) on a specific date.
Another name for the balance sheet, used because the statement reports a business’s financial position at a single point in time.
The date printed on a balance sheet that marks the exact moment, usually the close of business, whose financial position the statement reports.
An asset expected to be used up or converted to cash within one year, such as cash, accounts receivable, or inventory.
An asset expected to keep serving the business beyond one year, such as equipment, buildings, or land.
An obligation expected to be settled within one year, such as a short-term loan or unpaid supplier bills.
An obligation due more than one year out, such as a long-term loan or a mortgage.
The owners’ claim on the business, equal to what remains of the assets after subtracting what the business owes to others.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: The balance sheet is a photograph of a business taken at one exact moment. The camera catches everything the business owns — its cash, its stock of goods, its machines and buildings — on one side of the picture. On the other side it catches everything the business owes, plus what belongs to the owners. The two sides always match, because every thing the business has was paid for either with borrowed money (a liability) or with the owners’ money (equity). Items that will be used or paid within a year go in the current sections; everything else goes in the non-current sections. A fresh photograph is taken as of each reporting date, so you can compare one snapshot with the next to see how the business is changing.
eli10.analogy: Think of the balance sheet as a weigh station on a highway. A truck pulls in, and the scale records its load at that exact moment — one reading, not a log of the whole trip. The driver’s trip log (the income statement) tells you about the journey; the scale (the balance sheet) tells you how heavy the truck is right now. Owners and lenders both look at the scale reading, though they care about different parts of the load.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down because a truck’s weight is a fact you simply measure, while a balance sheet’s numbers are judgments made by accountants — what something is worth, how fast it will be used up, and which accounting rules the business chose. Also, a weigh station has one scale, but the same business can produce different snapshots under different rules, which is why comparing statements means knowing the rules behind them.

workedExample: Northgate Print Shop opens on March 1 with $25,000 in cash: $15,000 from owner Priya’s savings and a $10,000 bank loan. Priya buys a $12,000 printing press, $8,000 of paper and ink, and keeps $5,000 in cash. The balance sheet as of March 1 shows assets of $25,000 — the press ($12,000, non-current), inventory ($8,000, current), and cash ($5,000, current) — balanced against liabilities of $10,000 and equity of $15,000. The loan splits into $2,000 due within a year (current liability) and $8,000 due in three years (non-current). A lender reads $13,000 of current assets against $2,000 of current liabilities; Priya reads $15,000 of equity that is hers to keep growing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the balance sheet as if it covered a period
commonMistakes.correction: A balance sheet shows one moment; activity over time belongs on the income statement. Check the “as of” date and treat the statement as frozen at that instant.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a balanced sheet means a healthy business
commonMistakes.correction: The two sides match by construction for every business that keeps proper records, profitable or not. Balancing is arithmetic; look at what the numbers mean before judging.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sorting items by how long-term they feel instead of using the one-year rule
commonMistakes.correction: A machine headed for sale within a year is current, and a loan payment due in nine months is current even if the rest of the loan runs for years. Apply the one-year horizon to each item.
A balance sheet from six months ago may say nothing about today. Match the statement date to the question you are asking before drawing conclusions.

compareContrast.distinction: A snapshot of financial position at a single date versus a period report of revenues minus expenses over time.
Current items are expected to be used up, converted to cash, or settled within one year; non-current items operate on a horizon beyond one year.
One shows what the business has; the other shows who supplied it — creditors or owners — and the claims each holds.

keyTakeaway: A balance sheet is a snapshot of what a business owns, owes, and is worth on one specific date, with assets on one side and liabilities plus equity on the other — and because it always balances by construction, the real work is judging what the numbers mean.

questionBank.prompt: What does a balance sheet report?
options: A business's assets, liabilities, and equity at a single moment in time
A business's revenues and expenses over a period of time
The cash that flowed in and out during the year
The market value of the business's stock
questionBank.explanation: A balance sheet reports what a business owns (assets), owes (liabilities), and what is left for the owners (equity) on a specific date. Revenues and expenses belong on the income statement, cash flows belong on the cash flow statement, and stock price is a market figure, not a balance sheet line.
questionBank.skill: Identifying what the balance sheet reports

questionBank.prompt: A balance sheet is dated "as of June 30." What does that date tell you?
options: It covers the six months of activity ending June 30
It shows the financial position at the close of business on June 30
The business first opened its doors on June 30
All of the business's debts come due on June 30
questionBank.explanation: The "as of" date marks the exact moment the snapshot was taken: the balance sheet shows financial position at the close of business on that day. It does not summarize activity over time, mark the start of the business, or set a single due date for debts.
questionBank.skill: Interpreting the point-in-time nature of the balance sheet

questionBank.prompt: A delivery company holds $40,000 cash, $60,000 of customer invoices due within 60 days, and two loans: $15,000 due next March and $85,000 due in five years. Which items go in the current sections of its balance sheet?
options: Cash and the customer invoices only
The $15,000 loan due next March only
Cash, the customer invoices, and the $15,000 loan
Cash and the $85,000 five-year loan
questionBank.explanation: The current sections hold items that will be used up, converted to cash, or settled within one year. Cash and the customer invoices are current assets, and the $15,000 loan payment due within a year is a current liability; the $85,000 loan is non-current.
questionBank.skill: Classifying balance sheet items into current and non-current sections

questionBank.prompt: A lender must decide whether to give a bakery a one-year loan. Which reading of the bakery's balance sheet will the lender weigh most heavily?
options: The non-current assets, such as the building and the ovens
The owner's equity line on its own
The total of all long-term loans the bakery already carries
Current assets compared with current liabilities: what the bakery can turn into cash soon versus what it must pay soon
questionBank.explanation: A lender wants to know whether the bakery can pay what comes due within the loan's horizon, so it weighs near-term resources against near-term obligations. Buildings and ovens are long-term assets, equity alone does not show repayment capacity, and long-term loans miss the timing of the question.
questionBank.skill: Reasoning about what a lender looks for in the balance sheet

questionBank.prompt: Why does a balance sheet always balance, even for a business that is losing money?
options: Accountants adjust the numbers until the two sides happen to match
Assets equal liabilities plus equity by the design of the accounting system
Only businesses with balanced records are allowed to publish one
Auditors correct every statement before it is released
questionBank.explanation: The balance sheet is built from the accounting equation, so the two sides match by construction for any business that keeps proper records, profitable or not. No adjustment, permission, or audit is what makes it balance.
questionBank.skill: Explaining why the balance sheet balances by construction

provenance.rightsStatus: OpenStax Principles of Accounting, Volume 1 concepts adapted into original prose under CC BY 4.0 (no passages reproduced beyond short attributed phrases); CFI and SEC Investor.gov used as reference-only sources; no source prose reproduced
provenance.transformation: Balance sheet definition and snapshot framing (OpenStax 2.1, CFI Balance Sheet), the equation-in-statement shape (CFI Balance Sheet, CFI Accounting Equation), current vs non-current classification (OpenStax 2.2, CFI), statement-versus-period contrast (OpenStax 2.1, CFI Three Financial Statements), reader perspectives (CFI, OpenStax 2.2, SEC Investor.gov glossary), and the by-construction balancing framing (CFI) were synthesized from live source research. All names, scenarios, and arithmetic are original (Northgate Print Shop is a fictional business). The phase-2 machine-generated draft was treated as editorial intent only and no wording from it was carried over.
